title: a year of service designed
hook: twice the Gita describes people near the goal as delighting in the good of all beings
carry: whose good you'd be glad to see

segments.voice: Yesterday closed our re-reading of karma with the lotus leaf: in the water all day, and the water doesn't cling. When praise or blame landed on you, did it bead up, or soak in? Day nine hundred sixty-nine.

Sarvabhutahite ratah. A short Sanskrit phrase that turns up twice in the Gita, near the end of chapter five and again in chapter twelve, and both times it describes people who have come close to the goal. It means delighting in the good of all beings. Not putting up with it, not getting around to it: delighting in it. A few days ago we met King Janaka, who kept working for the holding together of the world. That was the duty side of acting for others. This phrase is the other side, the gladness in it. Over these six days, we're going to sketch a year of service, one piece at a time. Today, the reason under the whole thing.
screen: `TWICE IN THE GITA.` → `DELIGHTING IN THE GOOD OF ALL BEINGS.` → `SIX DAYS: A YEAR OF SERVICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the first place, in paraphrase. Near the end of chapter five, Krishna describes the sages who reach the peace of Brahman: their faults worn away, their doubts cut through, their selves held steady, delighting in the good of all beings. Then, in chapter twelve, Arjuna asks a different question. Which worshipers know yoga better, those who love God with a form, or those who seek the imperishable, beyond form? Krishna answers that those who fix their minds on him are the most devoted. But of the second group he says this: with the senses held in, even-minded everywhere, delighting in the good of all beings, they too come to me. Notice where the phrase sits. Not in a chapter on charity, and not in a list of rules. It sits inside portraits of people near the end of the path, as part of what they look like. On this reading, care for others isn't only a road toward the goal. It's one of the marks of having come close to it. That gives seva, a word Hindus use for service, a particular root. Not service as a good mood, or as an extra on a free weekend, and not a debt paid through gritted teeth. Service as something a settled heart is glad to do. And look at the word all. Not all who agree with me, not all in my family or my town. All beings. A temple kitchen feeding whoever walks in, a neighbor sitting with someone's parent, a person who sweeps the shared stairs because they're shared, someone who sets out water for birds in the heat: each one is the phrase made small enough to do. Which is why designing a year of service can start here, before any calendar or plan. The first question isn't what you'll do. It's whose good you'd be glad to see, and how wide that circle can go.
screen: `CHAPTER FIVE: THE SAGES NEAR THE GOAL.` · `CHAPTER TWELVE: THE SAME PHRASE.` · `CARE AS A MARK OF COMING CLOSE.` · `ALL BEINGS, NOT SOME.` · then, large: `WHOSE GOOD WOULD YOU BE GLAD OF?`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Start close. Bring to mind one person whose good you'd be glad to see today, and stay with them for a breath. Then widen the circle a little: a neighbor, a coworker, someone you pass often and don't really know. Then wider: a stranger in another city, an animal, a tree on your street. With each breath, let the circle open one ring further, and notice where gladness gets harder. Don't push past that place. Just mark it. Don't plan anything yet. If you pray, you can hold the whole circle before the one you pray to. The bell holds the time.
Sarvabhutahite ratah. Delighting in the good of all beings, a phrase from the Gita, said of those near the path's end.
Your line: whose good you'd be glad to see. Today, write down one person or creature, a little outside your usual circle, whose good you'd be glad to serve this year. Day nine hundred sixty-nine.

screen: `DAY 969 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A YEAR OF SERVICE DESIGNED.`

howItsDone: Seva, selfless service, takes forms such as cooking and serving food at temples, caring for elders and guests, cleaning shared spaces, and volunteering through community organizations.

fork.setup: Krishna is describing people who have come close to the goal. which mark does he name, in chapters five and twelve?
options: they have left all other people behind.
they delight in the good of all beings.
they care only for those who agree with them.
fork.reveal: Gita 5.25 and 12.4 both describe them as sarvabhutahite ratah, delighting in the good of all beings.

notes: Editor: hook and teach rebuilt. The draft repeated day 964 almost line for line (Janaka on the throne, lokasangraha, 'whatever a leading person does', Krishna needing nothing). The 'why serve' piece now rests on sarvabhutahite ratah, delighting in the good of all beings (Gita 5.25, 12.4), with Janaka only recalled; practice, word, carry, games, original and sources changed to match. The index word, title and carry are all 'a year of service designed' (days 969–974); the word screen and spoken word use the phrase as given. Suggest a real word (e.g. seva) in the outline.

Plan for the block: 969 lokasangraha (why serve), 970 svadharma (where), 971 the gift (Gita 17.20–22), 972 the guest (Taittiriya 1.11), 973 week end and abhyasa, 974 everything as offering (Gita 9.26–27).
